title: The chariot of the self
carry: the senses are horses; wisdom holds the reins
last: NOT BORN, AND DOES NOT DIE.

lines: HOME, WITH NO MEMORY OF THE DRIVE.
cards: Driving home, and arriving with no memory of the drive. Something got the car there, but who, exactly? Or the opposite: the plan was to go straight home, and somehow the car is in the drive-through line.
Who was steering? Yama knows the two paths are easy to name and hard to walk.
So he gives Nachiketa a picture to carry, with a place in it for every part of a person: the body, the mind, the senses, and someone riding along. A chariot.

teach.b: Know the self as the rider in the chariot, Yama says, and the body as the chariot. Know the buddhi, the intellect, the part of you that discerns and decides, as the charioteer. The manas, the everyday mind, is the reins.
The senses are the horses, and the things they chase are the roads. Picture them: sight, hearing, smell, taste, touch, each one strong, each pulling toward whatever it wants.
The reins connect them to the charioteer, and the rider is the one the whole trip is for. Then Yama says what goes wrong.
If the charioteer has no understanding, and the reins are always slack, the senses run wild like bad horses. That's the drive-through line.

If the charioteer understands and holds the reins steady, the senses are like good horses: all their strength, going where they should. Notice he doesn't say kill the horses. Horses are the power; you need them.
The point is who holds the reins.
And where does the road go? The one whose charioteer is wise, whose reins are steady, reaches the end of the road, which the text calls the highest place of Vishnu, the all-pervading.
It's one of Hinduism's clearest maps of a person: atman, body, buddhi, manas, senses.
And it's the two paths in one picture. The pleasant path lets the horses choose the road. The good path has the charioteer choose it, and the horses run there gladly.
Some readers hear an echo of it in the Gita, where Krishna is Arjuna's actual charioteer.

how: Hindu teachers of the Upanishads use the Katha's chariot to explain self, mind and senses, and some pair it with the Gita's picture of Krishna driving Arjuna's chariot.

o: a wheel, the turning of life

s: the Katha says to get rid of the horses
the horses are the power; the point is who holds the reins.
in the chariot image the mind is the reins
the manas is the reins; the intellect is the charioteer.
the road ends at the highest place of Vishnu
the all-pervading one, the text says.

games.q: you're the charioteer. the horses are pulling hard toward the pleasant road. what does Yama say a wise charioteer does?
o: holds the reins steady and chooses the road.
games.why: a charioteer with understanding holds the reins, and the senses become like good horses.

practice: Feel your senses as horses, and notice which one is pulling hardest right now: a sound, an itch, hunger, the phone.

Don't fight it; feel the reins in your hands and draw them in gently, not yanking, just steadying, until each horse settles. Then sit as the charioteer, reins held lightly, the rider behind you at rest.

wordCard.voice: Ratha, chariot. Know the self as the rider, the body as the chariot, the intellect as the charioteer, the mind as the reins, and the senses as the horses.

orig.note: Sanskrit: ratha, chariot; Katha 1.3.3: know the body as the chariot.
